                        Ice Sheet Dynamics and Climate Interactions in Sea Level Changes

MainThe Greenland ice sheet (GrIS) and the Antarctic ice sheet (AIS) hold most of the world’s land ice and freshwater (~58-m global mean sea-level equivalent (SLE) for AIS and ~7 m for GrIS)1,2,3. Recent observational estimates over the period 2002–2022 reveal that both are losing mass at rates of ~255 Gt yr−1 and ~127 Gt yr−1 (ref. 4), respectively, contributing a total of ~1.1 mm yr−1 to global sea-level rise. Anthropogenic greenhouse warming is expected to lead to substantial mass loss over large areas of the GrIS and AIS, as a result of increased ablation (including surface melt, basal melt and iceberg calving), which will probably outcompete the effect of increased snow accumulation due to higher moisture-holding ability of warmer air5, at least over the next centuries. However, considerable uncertainties remain in such century-scale projections6,7,8,9,10,11,12,13, which can be attributed to the representation of internal ice-sheet and ice-shelf processes (for example, ice rheology, grounding-line dynamics and basal melting), as well as the simulation of ice–ocean–atmosphere feedbacks.A missing piece in understanding ice-sheet sensitivity to increasing GHG concentrations is the long-term response of polar ice sheets on centennial to multimillennial timescales and their ability to either lose or sustain a substantial amount of ice under a given climate forcing. To study the long-term evolution of large ice sheets, such as the East AIS (EAIS), it is necessary to conduct multimillennial simulations14. Despite the importance of coupled climate–ice-sheet dynamics discussed in previous studies8,15,16,17,18,19, estimates of the long-term behaviour from coupled climate–ice-sheet models have so far been largely limited to Greenland8,20. Beyond this, long-term assessments have relied on either offline ice-sheet models that are forced by atmospheric and oceanic forcings and feedback parametrizations or simplified climate models. For example, based on simplified climate parametrizations in uncoupled ice-sheet simulations, it was reported that the West AIS (WAIS) might collapse if global warming relative to the pre-industrial (PID) levels exceeds the warming threshold (WT) of ~1–3 °C (refs. 10,21,22). The WT is a critical global mean temperature anomaly (relative to PID) at which positive or amplifying feedback processes (for example, melt–elevation feedback) accelerate ice loss10. The WT for the WAIS is mainly controlled by ice–ocean interactions (for example, ocean-driven basal melting and subshelf cavity warming), whereas ice–atmosphere interactions (for example, melt–elevation feedback) could become more important at higher thresholds, particularly for the EAIS12,22. The critical threshold leading to the complete melting of the EAIS has been estimated with an uncoupled ice-sheet model at ~6–10 °C (ref. 22) and WT estimates for an ice-free Greenland in offline and coupled models lie between ~0.8 °C and 5 °C (refs. 8,9,10,23).Coupled climate–ice-sheet feedbacks can regulate future ice-sheet loss, for example, (1) through ocean responses, such as meltwater-induced suppression of Antarctic bottom water formation and the intrusion of warm circumpolar deep water into subsurface ice-shelf cavities and the corresponding accelerated grounding-line retreat17,24,25 and (2) through atmospheric responses (cooling, changes in snowfall or clouds) to corresponding ocean or ice-sheet changes15, which can potentially slow down ablation processes. However, the relative importance of these processes depends on the timescale considered. Although ocean-driven processes strongly influence short-term ice-sheet loss, long-term ice-sheet evolution under sustained warming may become increasingly controlled by atmosphere-driven processes, which are the primary focus of this study.To date, long-timescale ice-sheet modelling studies have often used prescribed or simplified climate forcing22,23. Existing long-term coupled simulations for Greenland have primarily represented ice–atmosphere interactions, with ocean conditions either prescribed8 or evolving but coupled only in the ice-to-ocean direction20. Building on previous work, we examine the long-term response of the GrIS and AIS to increased CO2 concentrations within a coupled global climate–ice-sheet framework. To this end, we coupled the community Earth system model (CESM, version 1.2)26 with the bihemispheric Penn State University ice sheet–ice shelf model (PSUIM)27 (CPIM1; Methods; Supplementary Fig. 1). We conduct a series of idealized 100,000-year-long (100 kyr) CPIM1 simulations with stationary elevated CO2 concentrations (2 × CO2, 4×CO2, 6 × CO2, 8 × CO2 and 12 × CO2 relative to the PID levels) (Supplementary Table 1). We find that, unlike in uncoupled ice-sheet model experiments, the mass balance of the EAIS critically depends on atmospheric processes that substantially mitigate ice loss, resulting in much higher WT. These results provide insights into ice-sheet tipping points and the long-term legacy of human activities.Long-term ice-sheet responses to warmingCPIM1 uses the asynchronous coupling technique28,29,30 (Methods), in which we force in an alternating way the bihemispheric ice sheet for 1,000 years with a climatology that was obtained from a 10-year-long CESM1.2 model simulation, which has been forced by ice-sheet boundary conditions (Supplementary Fig. 1) from the previous ice-sheet modelling chunk. Using this technique, we obtained a quasi-equilibrium PID simulation with weak residual mass trends (Fig. 1a), spanning 100 kyr of the ice-sheet model and 1 kyr of CESM1.2 with a constant CO2 level of 285 ppm. Further details on the PID simulation are provided in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Figs. 2–6. Hereafter, the climatological mean of the PID simulation is referred to as the PID condition.Fig. 1: Greenland and AIS responses due to increasing CO2 concentration.Full size imagea, GrIS (upper plot) and AIS (bottom plot) volume changes (106 km3) in response to the PID condition and increasing CO2 concentrations (2 × CO2, 4 × CO2, 6 × CO2, 8 × CO2 and 12 × CO2). b–d, Simulated GrIS thickness of mean PID climatology (b), 4 × CO2 (c) and 12 × CO2 (d) experiments at the last time 100 kyr. e–g, Same as b (e), c (f) and d (g), but for AIS thickness. Maps in b–g created using Interactive Data Language (NV5 Geospatial).With increasing CO2 concentrations, the WAIS shows mass loss relative to the PID level, particularly over the marine-based regions of the ice sheet (Fig. 1e–g and Extended Data Fig. 1). Warming above 2 °C (relative to PID) induces substantial long-term ice volume loss over large areas of the GrIS and the WAIS (Fig. 2), corresponding to about 1-m and 2.5-m SLE, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 2). The estimated WT of 2 °C above PID levels for the WAIS agrees with previous studies22,31. The GrIS disintegrates when global warming exceeds ~6 °C (Fig. 2), broadly consistent with a possible WT of ~5 °C reported in a recent coupled modelling study8. The range in inferred WTs may be due to uncertainties in model climate sensitivities and differences in modelling setups. WTs inferred from coupled simulations tend to be larger than earlier estimates of 0.8–3.2 °C from standalone ice-sheet simulations23, probably because the spatially uniform climate forcing used in previous offline approaches does not fully capture regional temperature responses.Fig. 2: Global WTs of Greenland and AISs.Full size imageGrIS (grey-filled squares) and AIS (navy-filled circles) volume changes (106 km3) as a function of global mean surface air temperature changes in response to increasing CO2 concentrations (2 × CO2, 4 × CO2, 6 × CO2, 8 × CO2 and 12 × CO2) relative to the PID condition. Here global mean air temperature is used as a metric for the magnitude of global warming, as commonly adopted in WT studies. Each symbol represents a snapshot of the ice sheet at 1-kyr intervals. The final state of each CO2 sensitivity experiment is highlighted using filled symbols with black outlines.Whereas the GrIS shows a progressive retreat with rising temperatures and a complete disappearance in the 8 × CO2 experiment, the AIS appears to exhibit more step-like behaviour, which can be attributed to an initial disintegration of the marine-based WAIS and a subsequent thinning and retreat of marginal marine-basin ice in the EAIS (Fig. 1e–g and Extended Data Fig. 1). When the grounding line eventually reaches the terrestrial parts of the EAIS, the retreat and mass loss substantially slow down, even for continued exposure to 12 × CO2 conditions or global warming levels of 11 °C (Fig. 2). According to our coupled model experiments, the AIS remains surprisingly stable with a long-term mass loss of only ~6 m SLE (Extended Data Fig. 2). This result stands in sharp contrast to previous findings from uncoupled ice-sheet simulations22 that suggest a WT for Antarctica of 6–10 °C, beyond which a complete disintegration of the terrestrial eastern AIS could occur.Accumulation and ablation responses to warmingPotential factors contributing to the greater resilience of the EAIS include the increase of Antarctic precipitation due to the higher moisture-holding capacity in a warmer climate32, resulting from the nonlinear Clausius–Clapeyron (CC) relationship33 and the reduced ocean melting relative to the WAIS. Accumulation and ablation exhibit contrasting responses to increasing temperature (Fig. 3). Here accumulation includes snowfall and rainfall, whereas ablation includes surface melt, basal melt, iceberg calving and ice flow divergence. In the stable PID simulation, accumulation and ablation remain nearly balanced throughout, showing only a negligible difference (Fig. 3a,b). In contrast, the 12 × CO2 experiment initially exhibits greater ablation than accumulation during the first 10 kyr, before reaching an equilibrium state. This sustained excess of ablation over accumulation drives mass loss in both the GrIS and the AIS.Fig. 3: Accumulation and ablation changes due to increasing CO2 concentration.Full size imagea,b, GrIS (a) and AIS (b) accumulation (black in PID and red in 12 × CO2 experiment) and ablation (orange in PID and blue in 12 × CO2 experiment) changes (Gt yr−1). Accumulation includes rainfall and snowfall, whereas ablation includes surface melt, basal melt, iceberg calving and ice flow divergence. c,d, Grid-point-wise scatter plot of the first 10-kyr averaged changes in surface air temperature (K) and accumulation (%) relative to the PID for GrIS (c) and AIS (d) across all CO2 experiments. The red and blue lines indicate linear regression fits for the relationship: GrIS in red (c); West AIS (WAIS) in red and East AIS (EAIS) in blue (d) (Extended Data Fig. 3 shows the domains). The colour shading indicates the ice thickness changes relative to the PID. The inset map shows the accumulation change per degree of surface warming (% K−1). e,f, Same as c (e) and d (f) but for ablation changes (%). The first 10 kyr were used because the changes in accumulation and ablation are most pronounced during the initial adjustment, as shown in a and b. Maps in a–d created using Interactive Data Language (NV5 Geospatial).Percentage changes in accumulation and ablation per degree of local surface warming at each grid point are calculated from the first 10-kyr mean for different CO2 concentrations (Fig. 3c–f). Under warming, the GrIS loses mass and its ice elevation decreases (symbol shading in Fig. 3). Surface elevation lowering leads to additional ice-sheet warming and surface melting via the lapse-rate effect and is due to background atmospheric warming. The resulting ablation (sensitivity of ~12.2% K−1, Fig. 3e) is only partly compensated for by the warming-induced increase in accumulation, with a sensitivity of 7.2% K−1 (Fig. 3c). A similar behaviour can be observed for the WAIS (Fig. 3d,f), where ocean-driven ice loss leads to a massive drop in elevation, which increases both accumulation and ablation, with a larger increase in ablation (~6.8% K−1) than in accumulation (~3.9% K−1). However, for the EAIS, we find that accumulation increases more strongly with warming there (11.5% K−1 in accumulation but only 8.7% K−1 in ablation), which, over time, even leads to a thickening of some parts of the EAIS by a few hundred metres (symbol shading in Fig. 3d,f). It is worth noting that increased accumulation does not necessarily translate into ice mass gain because rainfall can enhance runoff, particularly over the GrIS and WAIS. In contrast, accumulation over the EAIS remains predominantly snowfall even under extreme warming, except for near-melting coastal regions (Supplementary Fig. 7).The stronger accumulation response relative to ablation reflects a higher precipitation sensitivity to warming, a characteristic found only in the EAIS. There are considerable orographically-driven differences in accumulation and ablation responses between the lower elevation coastal regions and the higher elevation inner plateau (inset map in Fig. 3d,f). The higher precipitation sensitivity in the inner EAIS is consistent with the limited role of ablation in the interior compared with the coastal regions34,35. Consistent with previous studies32,35, the continental-scale precipitation sensitivity is higher in the EAIS than the WAIS (Extended Data Fig. 3). The local precipitation sensitivity over the EAIS increases substantially with rising CO2 concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 8–10).Atmospheric controls on ice-sheet changesTo elucidate the underlying mechanisms for the regional precipitation enhancement, we determine the thermodynamic and dynamic (that is, changes in atmospheric circulation and moisture transport) contributions to temperature-scaled changes in precipitation (Methods). The most pronounced increases in precipitation occur over the Antarctic continent (Fig. 4a,b). A vital point to note is that the increase in precipitation in the Arctic is much smaller than that in Antarctica, even though both regions experience a substantial intensification of the thermodynamic contribution (Fig. 4c,d). The limited increase in Arctic precipitation is attributable to negative dynamical changes (that is, large-scale moisture divergence), which offset the thermodynamic effects (Fig. 4e,f). Unlike for the GrIS, the increasing total precipitation in the high-elevation region (>3 km) of the AIS arises from the combined and reinforcing influences of thermodynamic (~62%) and dynamic (~38%) changes. This indicates that changes in the atmospheric circulation, most notably a poleward shift of the westerlies (Fig. 5a), increase moisture convergence along the margins of the EAIS (Extended Data Fig. 5), thereby enhancing precipitation over the ice sheet.Fig. 4: Changes in precipitation due to increasing CO2 concentration.Full size imagea–f, Fractional changes of precipitation (snowfall + rainfall, %) between the 12 × CO2 sensitivity and the PID experiment in the Northern Hemisphere (a,c,e) and the Southern Hemisphere (b,d,f): total precipitation changes (ΔP) (a,b), CC-related thermodynamic changes (ΔPT) (c,d) and dynamic changes as a residual (ΔP − ΔPT) (e,f). The regions without × symbols indicate statistically significant differences at the 95% confidence level based on a two-sided t-test. Maps created using Interactive Data Language (NV5 Geospatial).Fig. 5: Changes in zonal wind, cloudiness and surface insolation due to increasing CO2 concentration.Full size imagea–c, Zonal wind at 850 hPa (a, m s−1), total cloud fraction (b, %) and surface insolation (c, W m−2) changes between the 12 × CO2 sensitivity and the PID experiment. The regions without × symbols indicate statistically significant differences at the 95% confidence level based on a two-sided t-test. The left insert panel shows the zonal mean changes in response to increasing CO2 concentrations (2 × CO2, 4 × CO2, 6 × CO2, 8 × CO2 and 12 × CO2) relative to the PID. Maps in a–c created using IDL V9.1. IDL is a registered trademark of NV5 Global, Inc.In addition to changes in precipitation, changes in surface insolation and their effects on ablation also need to be considered in the mass balance of ice sheets. Palaeoclimate studies reported that the transition of ice-sheet mass balance can be accelerated by surface insolation forcing36,37. In particular, global warming may increase cloud cover in high-latitude and polar regions, thereby reducing surface insolation in these areas38. Our simulations show that the CO2-driven changes in polar cloudiness and surface insolation are quite substantial and statistically significant at the 95% confidence level (Fig. 5b,c). The insolation pattern closely aligns with changes in cloud cover, exhibiting increased cloudiness of about 20–40% (Fig. 5b) and decreased insolation in polar regions with anomalies reaching up to 30 W m−2 (Fig. 5c). These effects become more pronounced as CO2 concentrations rise. The reduction in insolation subsequently affects the rates of land ice melting. Any decrease, or even a minor change, in surface insolation could reduce surface melting and the associated mass loss.To adequately account for such mitigating processes in ice mass loss, we performed additional offline ice model simulations that incorporated the climate effects of changes in snowfall and insolation. These sensitivity experiments are forced by the same climate forcings as the 12 × CO2 sensitivity experiment. A previous study using a coupled climate–ice-sheet model8 highlighted the effects of increased precipitation and reduced insolation on the ice mass balance. In GrIS, despite these negative climate feedbacks that could mitigate ice melting, the prevailing impact of surface warming leads to a substantial decrease in ice mass. Our simulation corroborates this conclusion for the GrIS, but yields contrasting results for the AIS.The offline ice model simulations, excluding the effects of both increased precipitation (ΔP = 0; the precipitation fixed at the PID value, thus excluding both thermodynamic and dynamic contributions) and reduced insolation (ΔS = 0), demonstrate a marked decline of ice volume in both GrIS and AIS (Fig. 6). The AIS experiences a more dramatic reduction of ~70% relative to its PID volume, in stark contrast to the 25% reduction in the coupled model simulation that includes dynamical changes in the atmospheric circulation and their impact on accumulation and surface melting (Fig. 6b). A previously overlooked feature is the substantially larger role of precipitation sensitivity in the coupled setup compared with the ablation over the EAIS (Fig. 3). We emphasize that the AIS has a more pronounced effect from precipitation (~54% reduction with ΔP = 0 only) than insolation (~29% reduction with ΔS = 0 only). In contrast, the insolation has a greater influence on the GrIS (Fig. 6a). Consistent with this result, the offline ice model simulations with prescribed ΔP and ΔS exhibit qualitatively similar ice-sheet responses to those obtained in the coupled climate–ice-sheet simulations. These results imply that, on long timescales and particularly under strong climate forcing, the imposed climate forcing exerts the dominant control on ice-sheet evolution. This further suggests that the stronger precipitation sensitivity in Antarctica may locally moderate ice loss under extreme warming scenarios.Fig. 6: Role of increasing precipitation and decreasing insolation on the ice-sheet viability.Full size imagea,b, Simulated GrIS (a) and AIS (b) volume changes (106 km3) relative to the PID (12 × CO2 sensitivity experiment, sky blue dots). In a, C denotes the climate forcing derived from the coupled simulation (that is, T for surface air temperature, P for precipitation and S for insolation), CPID the spatially varying PID climatology and ΔC the anomaly relative to CPID, where x, y and t denote the horizontal coordinates and time, respectively. To examine the respective effects of increasing precipitation (ΔP) and reduced insolation (ΔS) on the ice sheet, the results from standalone ice-sheet simulations without ΔS (orange dots), without ΔP (pink dots), without ΔS and ΔP (brown dots) and with ΔS and ΔP (red dots) are compared.DiscussionWe developed a coupled atmosphere–ocean–ice-sheet model, CPIM1, based on the CESM1.2 and the PSUIM. Our simulation offers insights into the long-term responses of the GrIS and AIS to increasing CO2 concentrations. We emphasized two climate processes that mitigate ice mass loss for the GrIS and AIS in response to rising CO2 levels: (1) an enhanced precipitation sensitivity due to the increased CC effect and moisture transport and (2) reduced insolation due to the increased formation of polar clouds. The former is particularly important for stabilizing the EAIS. Previous studies assumed constant precipitation sensitivities of 7.5% K−1 for GrIS23 and 5% K−1 for AIS22. However, our study demonstrated that the local precipitation sensitivity increases with elevated CO2 concentrations, in particular over the EAIS, where we observe a change at the EAIS ice core site from 10.9% K−1 for 2 × CO2 to 22.4% K−1 for the 12 × CO2 simulation (Extended Data Fig. 4). More importantly, recent observations support mass gain in the EAIS due to the recent increase in accumulation4,39,40, with a ratio of ~11% K−1 for 1970–202140 relative to the average of ~5.5% K−1 (ref. 35). The topographic features of the AIS facilitate greater moisture convergence (and thus more precipitation) along the coastal periphery of the EAIS, contributing to net mass gain across large parts of EAIS. Additional offline ice model simulations with CPIM1 (Fig. 6) provide further evidence of the role of precipitation in stabilizing the AIS, in contrast to the GrIS. This highlights the role of regional climate representations in understanding the long-term sensitivity of ice sheets.Previous offline modelling approaches have provided insights into identifying key dynamical processes which control local ice-sheet sensitivity and tipping behaviour31,41. However, the ability to assess the long-term reaction of the GrIS and AIS to persistent forcings remains limited because of uncertainties in how climate parametrizations represent evolving forcings over long timescales. To investigate this long-term ice-sheet response, we used a coupled modelling framework with relatively coarse spatial resolution and simplified representations of selected processes (for example, no explicit ice–ocean cavities and limited land-surface processes; Methods). Oceanic influences, including basal melting and calving (Supplementary Fig. 11), are included in the coupled framework, although their effects are not examined in detail here. Under extreme forcing (12 × CO2), subsurface Southern Ocean temperatures warm by up to ~7 °C (Extended Data Fig. 6d), which will accelerate basal melting. A sensitivity experiment with enhanced basal melt parametrization leads to more rapid Antarctic mass loss initially, but results in only minor differences in the long-term ice-sheet evolution (Supplementary Fig. 12).Our results contrast the conclusions from a previous coupled modelling study42 based on the iLOVECLIM Earth system model of intermediate complexity with prescribed climatological clouds and three vertical atmospheric layers coupled to the GRISLI ice-sheet model. iLOVECLIM simulates a low-albedo and more unstable EAIS, whereas the atmospheric circulation changes simulated in CPIM1, particularly the poleward migration of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies and the increase in cloudiness, may instead help maintain ice thickness and surface elevation over large parts of EAIS through sustained snowfall, snow cover and higher surface albedo. It is also worth noting that our standalone ice-sheet simulations do not produce a complete collapse of the EAIS, suggesting that differences in ice-sheet model configuration, in addition to atmospheric coupling, may contribute to the simulated EAIS resilience. These results highlight the potential value of coupled climate–ice-sheet frameworks for investigating long-term interactions, feedbacks and regional climate and sea-level dynamics.MethodsCoupled atmosphere–ocean–ice-sheet modelTo determine the long-term evolution of the polar ice sheets to various CO2 forcings, we coupled the CESM1.226 and three-dimensional ice-sheet–ice-shelf PSUIM27 (Supplementary Fig. 1), using an asynchronous coupled method28. The coupled model will be referred to as CPIM1. The CESM1.2 model is based on the CAM4 atmosphere model (T31, ~3.75° resolution, 26 vertical levels), the POP2 ocean model (gx3v5, 100 × 116 horizonal grids and 25 vertical levels), CLM4.0 land physics (T31, prescribed vegetation) and the CICE4 (gx3v5, Los Alamos sea ice model) sea ice components. The CESM configuration of our coupled CPIM1 simulations is identical to the setup described in a recent study43, including the model version (CESM1.2), horizontal resolution and physical parametrizations. This setup was shown to reproduce realistic large-scale temperature and precipitation patterns under palaeoclimate CO2 forcing, supporting its adequacy for providing polar climate forcing relevant to ice-sheet studies. Despite the relatively coarse resolution, our model is able to capture the large-scale circulation features, including the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and other key phenomena (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 13). The PSUIM represents the land ice-sheet–ice-shelf components for both the Northern Hemisphere (1.0° longitude × 0.5° latitude resolution) and the Southern Hemisphere (a stereographic grid with a 20-km resolution). Its performance has been described in recent studies15,30,44,45, demonstrating that the model reproduces key dynamical features of ice-sheet evolution, including nonlinear sensitivity and associated sea-level contributions across both hemispheres and a range of palaeo and future climate forcings, supporting the suitability of PSUIM for long-term ice-sheet sensitivity experiments.In the asynchronously coupled ice–climate framework, we integrated CESM for 10 years and PSUIM for 1,000 years in each coupling cycle, corresponding to a climate acceleration factor of 100 (defined as the ratio of CESM to PSUIM integration lengths). The coupling frequency between CESM and PSUIM is set to 1,000 years, achieved by applying the CESM-simulated climate of monthly surface air temperature, precipitation, surface shortwave radiation and annual mean 400-m subsurface ocean temperature to PSUIM. Subsequently, CESM is forced in return for 10 years by PSUIM-simulated ice-sheet cover, topography, surface roughness and freshwater fluxes. Specifically, the surface geopotential (PHIS) and topographic standard deviation (SGH) fields in CAM4, together with ice-covered surface conditions (for example, PCT_GLACIER) in CLM4.0, are updated at each coupling time step so that CESM experiences the effect of the evolving ice-sheet topography and associated surface changes.The coupled model uses a simplified bias correction approach for temperature and precipitation, using the ERA-5 reanalysis46 and Levitus ocean data47. Present-day climatological atmosphere and ocean temperature biases are corrected additively on the basis of differences from observations (anomaly-based correction), whereas precipitation biases are corrected multiplicatively using scaling factors derived from observations (Supplementary Fig. 14). The surface air temperature and precipitation from CESM are further downscaled to the high-resolution topography of PSUIM with lapse-rate corrections (γ = 5 °C km−1) and elevation–desertification correction. In the ocean, the model interpolates modern annual mean ocean temperatures at a depth of 400 m onto the ice-sheet model grid. In areas outside the spatial coverage of the ocean model grid, ocean temperatures are propagated beneath the ice shelves using a nearest-neighbour interpolation. The freshwater forcing from PSUIM runoff is applied to the CESM ocean grid cells along the ice-sheet perimeter and prescribed as virtual salinity fluxes to conserve ocean mass (therefore, sea level does not change explicitly in this setup of POP2). The liquid runoff (for example, basal melt and surface runoff) is routed directly to the nearest ocean grid points. Solid icebergs are considered as free-floating chunks of ice. They can drift and melt elsewhere, so the solid runoff (for example, calving of icebergs and cliff failure) from Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere ice sheets is converted into a homogeneous surface flux spread over the North Atlantic (50° N–70° N) and the Southern Ocean (poleward of 60° S). Although our coupled framework includes meltwater–ocean interactions, specific short-term feedbacks, such as meltwater-induced subsurface ocean warming and the amplification of subshelf melting48, are not explicitly isolated in the long-term diagnostics. This reflects the use of an asynchronous coupling strategy with 1,000-year ice–climate exchange intervals, a modelling choice intended to investigate millennial-scale ice-sheet responses rather than transient decadal feedbacks.PUSIM parametrizationsThe PSUIM calculates the surface mass and energy balances on the basis of the insolation–temperature melt model49. The net surface energy balance is calculated by the simplified equation:$${{\rm{d}}E}=\left(1-\alpha \right)Q+10T-m$$
                    (1)
                This includes the surface incoming shortwave radiation (first term, where Q is surface insolation and α is surface albedo) and a linear parametrization of the longwave radiation and turbulent heat exchanges (second term, where T is the daily mean temperature and m is a constant parameter). The parameter m was set here to 45 W m−2 in both Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The offline PSUIM also includes representations of the lapse-rate corrections (γ = 5 °C km−1) and elevation–desertification process due to atmospheric drying (CC factor of \({2}^{\frac{-\gamma \triangle H}{10\circ c}}\)) and parametrizations of calving hydrofracturing and marine ice-cliff failure, as well as inverse-derived basal sliding coefficients27,50. The CPIM1 in our study uses the same script-based, flexible coupling technique as the intermediate complexity model LOVECLIM–PSUIM15,30. In the coupling framework, the climate and ice-sheet models are run sequentially and linked through externally controlled coupling scripts. CESM-derived climate forcing is downscaled onto the higher-resolution PSUIM grid. Whereas CESM resolves melt by explicitly solving the full surface energy balance (including net radiation, latent and sensible heat fluxes), the surface mass balance in our simulation is calculated within PSUIM using a simple insolation–temperature melt scheme. Rain–snow partitioning is likewise diagnosed internally as a function of surface temperature. This approach allows surface mass balance to respond consistently to evolving, high-resolution ice-sheet topography within the ice model, while retaining the dominant thermodynamic controls on melt.The PSUIM does not explicitly resolve ocean circulation within ice-shelf cavities and instead represents sub-ice-shelf forcing through parametrized basal melt rates. Basal melting rates are calculated using a quadratic dependence on thermal forcing27, defined as the difference between the 400-m subsurface ocean temperature (TO; K) and the local freezing point temperature at a given depth (Tf). The resulting ocean-driven melt rate (OM) is given by:$${\rm{OM}}=\frac{{O}_{\rm{melt}}{K}_{\rm{T}}{\rho }_{\rm{w}}{c}_{\rm{w}}}{{\rho }_{\rm{i}}{L}_{\rm{f}}}\left|({T}_{\rm{O}}-{T}_{\rm{f}})\right|({T}_{\rm{O}}-{T}_{\rm{f}})$$
                    (2)
                where Omelt, KT, cw, ρw and ρi denote the oceanic melting parameter (Omelt = 1.0), transfer coefficient for sub-ice oceanic melting (15.77 m yr−1 K−1), specific heat of ocean water (4,218 J kg−1 K−1), density of ocean water and ice (1,028 kg m−3 and 910 kg m−3), respectively. We used a subsurface reference depth of 400 m to represent subsurface thermal forcing relevant for basal melting, consistent with previous studies6,51, as this depth broadly captures the level at which relatively warm subsurface waters interact with ice-shelf bases. The use of a fixed 400-m thermal forcing is a simplification, particularly for WAIS sectors where the grounding line deepens during retreat and may increasingly interact with warmer circumpolar deep waters. The 400 m simplification may, therefore, delay the timing of the grounding-line retreat and transient ice mass loss responses. However, given the multimillennial timescales in the present study and the vertically rather homogenous subsurface warming (~300–700 m) in the simulations (Supplementary Fig. 15), the main conclusions regarding long-term ice-sheet sensitivity are unlikely to depend on the choice of reference depth. Grounded basal melt is controlled by the basal energy budget, with melting occurring when combined geothermal heat flux and frictional heat inputs surplus conductive heat transfer through the ice.Ice-shelf calving occurs when surface and basal crevasses extend sufficiently to approach full-thickness penetration of the ice column. The model represents additional calving processes associated with hydrofracturing driven by surface meltwater and rainfall, as well as failure of tall ice cliffs linked to marine ice-cliff instability (MICI). The resulting penetration depth of water-filled crevasses, dw (m), is defined as:$${d}_{\rm{w}}={\rm{CREVLIQ}}\,{R}^{2}$$
                    (3)
                where CREVLIQ is set to 100 m−1 yr2 and R is the annual surface meltwater and rainfall (m yr−1). The MICI parametrization is applied with a maximum horizonal ice-cliff wastage rate (VCLIF) of 3 km yr−1.Glacial isostatic adjustment is represented using the elastic lithosphere–relaxing asthenosphere framework, assuming a spatially uniform flexural rigidity of 1025 N m, a bedrock density of 3,370 kg m−3 and a single mantle relaxation timescale of 3,000 years. Although this simplified treatment reproduces the effect of bed deformation induced by ice and ocean loading, it does not account for lateral variations in mantle viscosity. The grounding-line migration is determined by local flotation conditions: the grounding line retreats when ice thins to flotation and advances when ice thickens above flotation27. Ice flux across the grounding line is calculated using the Schoof flux parametrization52. This formulation permits dynamic grounding-line advance and retreat in response to evolving ice thickness, without requiring explicit front tracking. The hemispheric interactions are controlled through global sea-level change. Changes in eustatic sea level, computed from the combined bihemispheric ice-sheet volumes, influence ice-shelf dynamics by modulating the grounded and floating ice fluxes at the grounding line. The SLE changes are calculated using the standard volume-above-flotation approach, accounting for evolving bedrock topography and sea-level forcing, but without additional ocean volume or density corrections53.Ice dynamics are computed using a hybrid shallow-ice–shallow-shelf stress balance, with the shallow-ice approximation applied to grounded ice and the shallow-shelf approximation governing fast-flowing ice streams and floating ice shelves. Basal sliding is represented using a nonlinear stress–velocity relationship27, with spatially varying sliding coefficients. The sliding coefficients depend on homologous basal temperature and implicitly account for the effects of basal hydrology and substrate properties. In the Southern Hemisphere, sliding coefficients are obtained through a simplified inverse approach and constrained to the range from 10−10–10−5 m yr−1 Pa−2. In the Northern Hemisphere, a binary sliding scheme is adopted, assigning higher sliding values (10−6 m yr−1 Pa−2) to deformable marine sediments and lower values (10−10 m yr−1 Pa−2) to rigid continental bedrock30. The basal sliding coefficients are held fixed during the transient simulations, which represents a limitation of our approach and may preclude a more realistic representation of basal processes. Additional details of the PSUIM model configuration are described in a previous study27.Coupled climate–ice-sheet sensitivity experimentsThe coupled model is initialized independently in the climate and ice-sheet components. The climate component is branched after 2,300 years of a PID CESM1.2 control run, which serves as the initial condition for all PID and CO2 sensitivity experiments. In contrast, the ice-sheet initial state is taken from a previously published, quasi-equilibrated 8,000-year LOVECLIM–PSUIM simulation15. These spin-up simulations exhibit minimal long-term drift in both climate and ice volume under fixed PID forcing (Supplementary Fig. 16). Our simulations are then integrated for 100,000 years with constant CO2 forcing, allowing for the quasi-equilibration of all climate system components. To reduce computing time, we applied a climate acceleration factor of 100 to the CESM run, compressing the simulation time to 1,000 years in CESM (compared with 100,000 years in PSUIM). The PID control simulation is performed with atmospheric CO2 concentration of ~285 ppm (PID level). The warming simulations (CO2 sensitivity experiments) also apply constant CO2 values (2 × CO2, 4 × CO2, 6 × CO2, 8 × CO2 and 12 × CO2, relative to the PID condition) (Supplementary Table 1). Owing to the 1,000-year coupling frequency, the climatic conditions and ice volumes from sensitivity experiments are averaged over 1,000 years. Unless otherwise noted, results from the last 10 kyr of each sensitivity simulation are averaged and expressed as anomalies relative to the PID control mean. Statistical significance is assessed using two-sided t-tests (100 samples for PID and 10 samples for each sensitivity simulation). Using the PID climatological mean ensures a consistent reference for comparing spatial patterns across experiments, with results insensitive to the use of the PID end-state instead (Supplementary Fig. 17).On long timescales, the climate and ice-sheet responses are primarily driven by sustained CO2 forcing rather than by transient adjustments to small perturbations in the initial conditions. We also ignore orbital changes in insolation due to the dominant Milankovitch cycles. Accordingly, instead of adopting an ensemble approach, we conducted a suite of additional sensitivity simulations to assess the robustness of our results to key model parameters and coupling choices. Lapse-rate-based precipitation corrections can substantially influence melt–elevation feedbacks, with sensitivities potentially depending on model configuration and coupling framework details54. Although hydrofracturing and MICI parametrizations are included to capture plausible high-end calving responses under extreme climate forcing, these processes remain uncertain55.Sensitivity experiments explore the effects of (1) atmospheric parametrizations applied to the ice sheet, including precipitation correction and a lapse rate of 8 °C km−1 (Supplementary Fig. 18), (2) ocean related parameters controlling hydrofracturing (CREVLIQ = 100) and MICI (VCLIF = 0), as well as basal ocean melting rates (that is, Omelt = 2.0; Supplementary Fig. 12), (3) initial ice-sheet geometry (Supplementary Fig. 19) and (4) ice–climate coupling frequency (Supplementary Fig. 20). The experiments indicate that lapse-rate-based precipitation corrections can substantially influence melt–elevation feedbacks (Supplementary Fig. 18). In particular, a larger lapse-rate correction (8 °C km−1) produces a greater reduction in AIS volume through enhanced elevation-dependent warming. Ocean-parameter sensitivity experiments show more rapid ice loss under enhanced basal melting, whereas hydrofracturing and MICI parametrizations lead to additional AIS loss (Supplementary Fig. 12). Variations in the initial ice-sheet geometry produce only modest differences in the simulated response (Supplementary Fig. 19). In addition, simulations using shorter coupling intervals without climate acceleration and longer CESM integration periods (reducing the climate acceleration to 10) exhibit faster early-stage ice loss due to more rapid ocean adjustment, while the final ice-sheet states remain very similar to those obtained in the default configuration (Supplementary Fig. 20). All parameter sensitivities show comparable results.Standalone ice-sheet sensitivity experimentsTo examine the respective effects of insolation and precipitation sensitivity on ice viability, we performed standalone ice model simulations using climate forcing from the coupled climate–ice model run with a 12 × CO2 concentration (12CO2_L8; using the lapse rate of 8 °C km−1), the results of which are shown in Fig. 6. One ice model offline simulation applied the same configuration as the coupled run, including identical precipitation and insolation changes (ΔP and ΔS). Other offline simulations used the same configuration, but without explicit changes in insolation (ΔS = 0), precipitation (ΔP = 0) or both (ΔS = 0 and ΔP = 0).Precipitation sensitivity to temperature changesPrecipitation sensitivity to temperature changes is quantified using two different diagnostics. At continental and ice-sheet scales, sensitivity is estimated from the regression slope between precipitation and surface air temperature anomalies (dP/dT, regression-based sensitivities; Extended Data Fig. 3). At the local grid scale, spatial patterns of sensitivity are quantified separately for each CO2 experiment using the differences between the CO2 and PID experiments, defined as ΔP/ΔT (local precipitation sensitivities; Supplementary Figs. 8,9c and 10c and Extended Data Fig. 4). Here precipitation anomalies are expressed as percentage changes relative to the PID mean, such that both estimates are shown in % K−1 to facilitate comparison with CC scaling. The temperature and precipitation changes are also examined at representative local sites over the GrIS (North Greenland Ice Core Project site; 75° N, 42° W) and WAIS (WAIS Divide site; 79° S, 112° W) and EAIS (Dome Fuji site, 77.32° S, 39.7° E).Thermodynamic and dynamic contributions to precipitationWe calculate (1) the total relative precipitation change in the 12 × CO2 experiment relative to PID (ΔP; %), (2) the one related to the CC thermodynamic contribution (ΔPT) and (3) the dynamic contribution to precipitation (ΔPdyn) (Fig. 4). The thermodynamic changes are simply calculated as follows33,56:$$\Delta {P}_{\rm{T}}={M}^{* }\Delta {q}_{\rm{cc}}$$
                    (4)
                where M* is the PID ratio of precipitation to specific humidity (that is, P/q), CC-related specific humidity is qcc = 0.622Es/(1,000.0 − Es) (with Es = 6.1094 × 10[17.625T/(T+243.04)] in the August–Roche–Magnus approximation) and Δ is the difference between the 12 × CO2 and the PID experiment. The thermodynamic changes reflect local surface temperature variations arising from climate radiative forcings, temperature advection and temperature adjustments due to regional ice elevation changes. The dynamical changes are quantified here as residual anomalies between ΔP and ΔPT and mostly originate from circulation-driven changes in the convergence of the moisture flux.Limitation of the modelling frameworkWe used relatively coarse resolution and simplified representations of selected processes. These choices limit the ability to capture localized and transient ice–ocean interactions, particularly within narrow subshelf cavities, which may affect the timing and pathways of ice-sheet retreat57. In addition, coarse-resolution ice-sheet models may exhibit a delayed dynamic response to ocean forcing58. Higher spatial resolution would therefore be required to more accurately represent regional climate conditions and local grounding-line and outlet glacier dynamics. Previous studies have also suggested that more realistic representations of vegetation and land-surface processes may further accelerate GrIS retreat and potentially influence the estimated WTs20,59. Other processes that need to be considered in future coupled modelling studies include glaciogenic dust mobilization60 and the formation of proglacial lakes61.

items.body:
Gli alberi e il clima della città                
												
																																	                
					Ott 7, 2026Ott 31, 20265 commenti su Gli alberi e il clima della città

Il prof. Stefano Mancuso è molto noto al pubblico italiano grazie ad una serie di libri, articoli sui giornali e numerose conferenze tenute in tutto il paese, in cui propone gli alberi come principale risposta alla crisi climatica. Siamo sicuramente d’accordo che gli alberi nelle città siano molto utili; e va anche detto che Mancuso ha il merito di contribuire a diffondere la consapevolezza del problema del riscaldamento globale presso un pubblico molto ampio. Proprio per questo, e per l’ascolto che ha, presso gli amministratori e gli opinionisti, le cose che dice vanno prese sul serio e verificate. Dispiace quindi dover dire che diverse sue affermazioni non reggono a una verifica scientifica.

I combustibili fossili sono la questione principale

Su Climalteranti abbiamo già discusso alcune sue argomentazioni (qui nel 2020 e qui nel 2023), in particolare evidenziando l’inconsistenza della proposta, molto pubblicizzata, di “piantare mille miliardi di alberi” per “salvare il clima” o addirittura per “guadagnare 10 anni nella lotta al cambiamento climatico”. Pur riconoscendo ovviamente i benefici degli alberi e delle foreste, le critiche vertevano sia sull’impossibilità pratica di attuare programmi così vasti, sia sull’effetto marginale che queste piantagioni avrebbero sul clima: perché almeno tre quarti delle emissioni climalteranti dipendono dall’immenso (ab)uso di combustibili fossili, le cui emissioni storiche di CO2 possono essere assorbite in minima parte dagli alberi.

Sul fronte della mitigazione, quindi, il contributo degli alberi in ambito urbano non potrà che essere modesto: la CO₂ che assorbono è poca cosa rispetto a quella emessa da una città, e il bilancio netto delle forestazioni urbane, una volta considerate le emissioni legate alla messa a dimora, all’irrigazione e alla manutenzione, è marginale.

La necessità di ridurre drasticamente e rapidamente l’uso dei combustibili fossili non può in alcun modo essere compensata dal piantare alberi (si veda qui).

Alberi e adattamento

Più recentemente, con un articolo su Repubblica del 22 settembre e con interventi video, come quello qui disponibile sul sito dello stesso quotidiano, Mancuso ha invece proposto gli alberi come la principale azione di adattamento ai cambiamenti climatici per la città.

Gli alberi e il verde possono contribuire in modo significativo all’adattamento urbano. Ad esempio, in un ampio studio recentemente apparso su “Nature Communications” si legge:

“Gli alberi raffrescano l’ambiente grazie all’evapotraspirazione, che favorisce la dissipazione del calore, e all’ombreggiamento, che riduce la radiazione solare incidente e il conseguente assorbimento di calore da parte di superfici come asfalto e calcestruzzo. Complessivamente, questi due fenomeni riducono la temperatura dell’aria (AT) in media di 1–2 °C direttamente sotto un filare di alberi stradali, secondo una rassegna di studi basati su misurazioni in loco dell’effetto refrigerante della vegetazione urbana”.

Una strada su sei

Se quindi è sicuramente condivisibile che le alberature possono essere utili per ridurre l’isola di calore urbana, Mancuso va molto oltre, scrivendo che “la quantità di alberi presente nelle città rappresenterà il discrimine principale fra adattarsi al riscaldamento globale o subirne le conseguenze”, e lanciando quindi agli amministratori pubblici la proposta-appello di sostituire il 15% delle strade delle città con piantagioni di alberi.

Non sono forniti studi a supporto della scelta del 15% al posto del 5% o 10% o 20%. La cifra è buttata un po’ come un numero magico, come del resto erano i “1000 miliardi di alberi”. A volte il 15% non è delle strade ma dell’asfalto, e non è chiaro se nel 15% debbano quindi essere conteggiati i tanti sottofondi stradali in porfido; o se marciapiedi, piste ciclabili, piazze e incroci debbano essere conteggiati.

Sottrarre alla viabilità il 15% delle strade, ossia poco meno di una strada su sei, per chi conosce come funziona una città e la sua mobilità, è un obiettivo chiaramente irrealizzabile. Basta provare a scegliere mentalmente le vie intorno a casa propria: una via su sei trasformata in un’area alberata. Il motivo è che le strade non sono tracciate a caso e non servono solo alle auto (molte delle quali, certo, potrebbero sparire): danno accesso ad abitazioni, garage e passi carrai, negozi e attività produttive, mezzi di soccorso; sotto di esse corrono i sottoservizi (acqua, fognature, gas, elettricità, fibra), con caditoie e pozzetti che mal convivono con gli apparati radicali. Mentre togliere la sosta delle auto sulla  strada è una cosa giusta e fattibile, pur essendo politicamente molto difficile, come sa chiunque ci abbia provato, è impossibile delocalizzare gli accessi alle abitazioni: eliminare un sesto della rete stradale è tutt’altra cosa.

Nelle proposte di Mancuso appare evidente la tendenza a semplificare troppo, proponendo soluzioni rapide e miracolose che piacciono tanto a giornalisti e politici (e anche al pubblico), trascurando le alternative, e l’analisi dei costi e dei benefici. L’adattamento delle aree urbane prevede indubbiamente il potenziamento del verde, ma si tratta anche qui di un tassello, utile ma certo non risolutivo, in un puzzle molto più ampio che deve includere non la forestazione dell’intera strada, ma anche altri tipi di ombreggiamenti, ad esempio con tendoni, la predisposizione di rifugi climatici e di zone raffrescate con altri sistemi, e soprattutto la ristrutturazione energetica degli edifici privati e pubblici.

Va ricordato che, in molti contesti dei centri storici, tipici di tantissime città, l’impossibilità di effettuare piantumazioni e depavimentazioni è legata a vincoli storici o architettonici, o alla presenza di infrastrutture sotterranee. Ad esempio, a  Madrid (nella foto) questi vincoli hanno portato in diversi casi ad optare per tendoni ombreggianti.

Non basta il coraggio

Nel video, Mancuso sostiene che per rimuovere il 15% dell’asfalto delle strade servano solo amministratori coraggiosi. Non è così. Servirebbero risorse ingentissime (progettazione, spostamento dei sottoservizi, depavimentazione, messa a dimora, irrigazione e manutenzione per decenni) e uffici tecnici con molto più personale di quello attuale; i Comuni italiani sono spesso affetti da una carenza di personale e va ricordato che, al contempo, dovrebbero portare avanti la riqualificazione energetica di scuole ed edifici pubblici. È quindi sbagliato presentare come una questione di volontà ciò che è soprattutto una questione di soldi, competenze e tempi.

C’è poi la questione dei benefici. Come riporta la rassegna citata, un filare di alberi riduce la temperatura dell’aria di 1-2 °C direttamente sotto le chiome, con effetti che si attenuano nello spazio circostante. Nell’articolo di Mancuso sono citati numeri molto più alti di riduzione, 5-6 °C, e  nella comunicazione pubblica si arriva anche a 10 °C, spesso frutto della confusione tra la temperatura dell’aria e quella delle superfici; quest’ultime hanno variazioni molto maggiori di quelle dell’aria. Ombra ed evapotraspirazione sono benefici reali, ma quando una massa d’aria rovente staziona sull’intera Pianura Padana o sulla conca fiorentina, stare sotto un albero o in un giardino pubblico non cambia di molto l’esposizione al caldo; e soprattutto non cambia la temperatura all’interno delle case, dove si trascorre la maggior parte del tempo e dove sono esposte al caldo le persone più fragili. Scrivere che «la quantità di alberi presente nelle città rappresenterà il discrimine principale fra adattarsi al riscaldamento globale o subirne le conseguenze» è quindi fuorviante: fa credere che una sola misura basti a mettere una città al riparo dal caldo.

Il rischio è che amministratori e politici inseguano la ricetta semplice e trascurino i piani di adattamento ben strutturati, in cui ogni azione è valutata in base a costi, efficacia e fattibilità, e in cui il verde è una componente importante, ma spesso non la principale.

I pericoli delle semplificazioni seducenti

Il problema della semplificazione non è solo quantitativo. Davanti a un rischio complesso tendiamo a compiere un gesto e a sentirci a posto (gli psicologi lo chiamano single action bias), e piantare un albero è il gesto perfetto: naturale, visibile, apparentemente gratuito.

La grande efficacia comunicativa di Mancuso poggia anche su scorciatoie che rendono le sue tesi più seducenti che fondate. Le sue piante «decidono», «ricordano», «comunicano»: è vero che producono segnali elettrici, orientano le radici verso l’acqua, rispondono agli attacchi dei parassiti, ma chiamare «decisione» un tropismo e «memoria» una traccia chimica significa usare le parole della mente per processi che di una mente non hanno bisogno, ed è proprio sul vocabolario, più che sui dati, che la fisiologia vegetale lo contesta da anni. A questo si aggiungono un gergo mutuato dalle neuroscienze («neurobiologia vegetale», «cervello diffuso») che fa sembrare solide spiegazioni che non aggiungono nulla, un frame apocalittico che colpisce ma non aiuta a scegliere, e storie raccontate magistralmente, che trasportano l’ascoltatore e lo rendono meno incline a cercare obiezioni. Lo stesso schema si ritrova nelle proposte sulla città: una soluzione semplice, naturale ed emotivamente appagante, che sorvola su numeri, costi e vincoli.

Il gesto visibile e suadente non si limita a sostituire l’azione più difficile, ne offre anche l’alibi: chi ha piantato l’albero si sente già a posto con la coscienza. La narrazione consolatoria, in questo, è più insidiosa delle forzature scientifiche che la veicolano. Non ci inganna solo su cosa siano le piante, ma su cosa basti fare per il clima. E sposta l’attenzione da ciò che dovremmo smettere di fare.

Non slogan accattivanti, ma proposte ragionate e fondate

Tutti siamo d’accordo che sia cruciale conservare e curare attentamente il patrimonio arboreo già esistente nelle città, aumentare notevolmente il verde e il numero di alberi liberando le strade dalle auto, perseguendo piani ambiziosi. Ma riteniamo che agli amministratori vada proposta non “la soluzione” per l’adattamento, ma una gamma ragionata e documentata di soluzioni per ridurre l’impatto del nuovo clima sulle città e sui loro cittadini.

Nella ricetta per non subire le conseguenze del riscaldamento globale deve trovare posto anche la mitigazione, che costituisce la strategia prioritaria da perseguire nella lotta contro il cambiamento climatico. Né si può dire che la mitigazione sia sottintesa: una narrazione che non la nomina rischia di farla passare in secondo piano e di fornire un ulteriore alibi all’inattivismo, di cui abbiamo parlato in numerosi post.

items.body:
Il metodo scientifico contro il negazionismo climatico                
												
																																	                
					Set 14, 2026Set 15, 20262 commenti su Il metodo scientifico contro il negazionismo climatico

Il consenso scientifico sul ruolo umano nel riscaldamento globale nasce da oltre un secolo di ricerca e confronto tra ipotesi alternative. Il metodo scientifico non richiede che ogni teoria venga discussa all’infinito: quelle smentite dai dati vengono progressivamente abbandonate.

Anche le spiegazioni alternative del riscaldamento attuale sono state studiate, senza trovare evidenze sufficienti a sostenerle. Il confronto avviene attraverso la ricerca pubblicata a valle della revisione tra pari. Considerare accertata l’origine antropica del riscaldamento globale è quindi il risultato del metodo scientifico, non la sua negazione.

Peraltro, in questo caso non si tratta di un semplice dibattito scientifico fine a sé stesso, bensì di qualcosa che sottende una serie di azioni di mitigazione che devono essere messe in campo al più presto, senza ulteriori tentennamenti.

Al di là degli errori marchiani nei grafici di Franco Battaglia pubblicati su La Verità (si vedano i precedenti post qui e qui), l’articolo pubblicato il 2 agosto contiene altre affermazioni gravi che purtroppo spesso si sentono nel dibattito sul clima.

Battaglia ha accusato due fisici e climatologi, Bruno Carli e Filippo Giorgi, di non seguire il metodo scientifico, in quanto hanno dichiarato inequivocabile il ruolo antropico sull’attuale cambiamento climatico, hanno citato i rapporti dell’IPCC, e hanno sostenuto che è chiuso il dibattito sulle cause delle variazioni climatiche attuali. La comunità scientifica, secondo Battaglia, rinnegherebbe in questo modo il metodo galileiano perché rifiuterebbe di confrontarsi in dibattiti pubblici con chi nega le cause umane, e pertanto non conoscerebbe le critiche che questi muoverebbero.

In realtà il dibattito sulle cause del riscaldamento globale è veramente chiuso, e ci sono anche molti altri campi della scienza in cui lo è. Praticamente nessuno dubita che molte malattie siano dovute ad infezioni batteriche o virali, che la radioattività sia dovuta a decadimenti nel nucleo dell’atomo, che la gravità sia dovuta alle deformazioni dello spaziotempo descritte dalla relatività generale, che gli organismi viventi cambino nel tempo soggetti ai meccanismi dell’evoluzione descritti da Charles Darwin, che la Terra abbia circa 4,7 miliardi di anni, che i continenti si muovano secondo la tettonica a zolle, che l’Universo sia in espansione. In tutte queste affermazioni ci sono punti oscuri, cose che possono lasciare qualche appiglio a chi voglia proporre alternative. La relatività generale potrebbe essere sostituita da teorie più ampie, l’evoluzione darwiniana potrebbe essere integrata da altri meccanismi, ma il quadro generale difficilmente cambierà. Questo significa che un astrofisico che consideri “chiuso” il dibattito sull’espansione dell’Universo stia rigettando il metodo scientifico? Che non conosca le teorie alternative proposte? In realtà queste teorie trovano spazio nelle riviste del settore, ma semplicemente non riescono a convincere se non una ristrettissima minoranza dei ricercatori, oltre ad essere spesso pure in contrasto tra di loro.

In effetti il cuore della mentalità scientifica è la libertà di pensarla diversamente, di esplorare strade nuove, di proporre visioni alternative. Ogni volta che si apre un problema scientifico emergono voci discordanti e ogni scienziato esplora quella per lui più promettente. Molti ricercatori si accodano a quelle più gettonate, ma altri sanno benissimo che il loro successo dipende dalla capacità di smentire la visione in quel momento dominante e proporne una migliore. Ma via via che le ricerche proseguono, alcuni rami vengono tagliati. Ci si accorge che non portano da nessuna parte, che le premesse non erano corrette, e soprattutto che le ipotesi non reggono alla prova dei fatti. Il consenso si forma in questo modo, per eliminazione di tante ipotesi logiche, magari plausibili, ma purtroppo sbagliate.

C’è sempre la possibilità che emerga una nuova ipotesi che spieghi meglio i fatti, succede: ma man mano che la teoria si afferma, questo diventa però sempre più difficile e più raro. La teoria rimasta ha assorbito parte di quelle concorrenti, ha eliminato, grazie anche alle loro critiche, alcuni aspetti sbagliati, e finisce per coprire un ambito molto più vasto di quello del problema originale, per cui ogni nuova teoria si troverà a dover spiegare un insieme di fenomeni molto grande in modo altrettanto accurato.

Negli esempi fatti, come per l’origine antropica dell’attuale cambiamento climatico, il dibattito c’è già stato, e dopo oltre un secolo di fuoco incrociato queste teorie hanno una solidità che richiede argomentazioni molto forti, e dati che oggi semplicemente non esistono, per essere contestate. In futuro potranno emergere nuove evidenze, e il dibattito si riaprirà. Non oggi. E molto difficilmente alcune conclusioni di base, come appunto l’origine antropica del riscaldamento globale, verranno modificate, in quanto sostenute da una conoscenza solida della fisica del clima alla base e da una quantità di dati immensa che conferma la teoria. Ogni teoria alternativa avrebbe quindi il problema di dover incorporare anche questi dati e queste evidenze. Ogni solida teoria, anche quelle citate sopra, avrà comunque sempre qualche rompiscatole irriducibile, che continuerà a cercare di scovare ed evidenziare punti deboli. E per fortuna i rompiscatole esistono, perché i punti deboli li vedi male dall’interno, e l’evidenziarli ha consentito alle teorie di raffinarsi, correggere errori, e diventare più solide.

Un esempio classico, per tornare al clima, è l’ipotesi avanzata dall’astrofisico Svensmark, di un influsso sul clima dei raggi cosmici. Un maggior flusso di particelle cariche, non schermate dal vento solare, potrebbe favorire la formazione di nuvole, alterando la quantità di radiazione solare che queste riflettono. I dati che Svensmark portava indicavano questa possibilità, che venne presa seriamente in considerazione, al punto che il CERN mise in piedi un esperimento dedicato, in cui raggi cosmici artificiali interagivano con nubi artificiali in una grande camera, per studiare il fenomeno. Abbiamo imparato diverse cose, ma l’ipotesi originale è stata smentita. Nel frattempo, la correlazione trovata da Svensmark tra flusso di raggi cosmici e nubi è stata pure smentita da nuovi dati. Questo non ha convinto l’astrofisico, che continua a sostenere la sua ipotesi, ma ha convinto tutti gli altri. Il dibattito su questo punto si è dunque chiuso.

In ogni caso il dibattito scientifico non si fa sui quotidiani o nelle conferenze pubbliche. La scienza si fa su riviste “peer reviewed” (ovvero soggette a revisione tra pari), in cui esporre le proprie ipotesi e presentare i propri dati. Per pubblicare occorre tuttavia passare un filtro, dei colleghi cercheranno di valutare la correttezza formale dell’articolo proposto, se i dati supportano le conclusioni; ad esempio, usare un grafico fermo al 1855 su scala locale, per sostenere che nel 2000 non ci sia stato un aumento di temperatura globale particolarmente rilevante, non verrebbe accettato, sarebbe rigettato senza pietà. Anche la riproposizione di argomenti già presentati e ripresentati non è sufficiente alla pubblicazione, servono argomenti nuovi. Non si tratta di una censura contro le idee innovative, anche perché con l’elevato numero di riviste scientifiche esistenti sarebbe praticamente impossibile imporla. Semmai esiste il problema opposto: oggi diverse riviste accettano per la pubblicazione, a pagamento, anche articoli di qualità molto scadente.

Alla fine, gli articoli che criticano l’origine umana del riscaldamento globale sono pochissimi, tra quelli recenti circa 1 ogni 200 che invece lo sostengono, un centinaio in tutto tra gli 88 mila articoli di climatologia pubblicati nell’ultimo decennio, ma proprio per quello non passano inosservati. Qualsiasi climatologo conosce molto bene quelli che per Battaglia sarebbero “i fatti che lo sconfessano”. Nei post di Climalteranti molti di questi sono già stati discussi. Esistono in rete siti dedicati in cui ciascuno di questi “fatti” viene analizzato, ed è possibile esaminare le argomentazioni e gli articoli scientifici pro e contro. Insomma, il dibattito è chiuso perché le argomentazioni sono state prese in considerazione, analizzate, e rigettate in base ai dati disponibili.

Le cose vanno molto peggio per chi opera ormai fuori dal mondo accademico, come Franco Battaglia, che sostiene che il riscaldamento in atto non abbia un’origine antropica riproponendo grafici fermi al 1850, curve di assorbimento interpretate male, grafici che mostrano un aumento della temperatura per sostenere che questo aumento non ci sia, calcoli sballati di equilibrio radiativo, errori marchiani di calcolo, e tanti altri dati sbagliati e fraintendimenti di cui solo in parte abbiamo avuto tempo (e voglia) di occuparci in queste pagine.

Infine, poco sensate sono anche le accuse all’IPCC, che certamente segue il metodo galileiano. È un organismo che passa in rassegna le conclusioni di tutti gli articoli, anche di quell’1 su 200 contrario, e cerca di sintetizzare le conclusioni. Anzi, lavorando su un consenso, dà un peso molto maggiore a chi è più prudente relativamente agli impatti degli scenari futuri, si presentano solo gli effetti che sostanzialmente tutti ritengono realistico aspettarci. Ma essere galileiani non significa dare lo stesso peso al geocentrismo rispetto all’eliocentrismo. E continuare a spiegare le “ragioni” del geocentrismo fa un pessimo servizio a chi ascolta.

Post scriptum: i due fisici criticati da Battaglia per non essere scienziati dispongono delle seguenti credenziali bibliometriche Scopus (aggiornate ad agosto 2026):

Filippo Giorgi: 386 articoli, 47403 citazioni, h-index 111

Bruno Carli: 127 articoli, 1805 citazioni, h-index 23

A titolo di confronto, Franco Battaglia dispone di 27 articoli, quasi tutti precedenti al 1993 (33 anni fa) e nessuno inerente temi riconducibili al riscaldamento globale o i temi ambientali, 168 citazioni, h-index 8
